title: AI Agents & Leadership
intro: Level 4 of the ByteBusters Generative AI Journey: you learn to direct AI agents that take actions, with humans approving, checking and staying in charge. You'll also lead: research AI and jobs in Nigeria, teach younger pupils, write your club's AI rules and defend a capstone for a real local need.
termProject: A capstone AI project for a real local need (e.g. a rain-check and spraying-tip tool for small farmers near Ilaro), planned with an agent-style step list, human approval, verified outputs and real-user testing, then defended with the 5 signs of understanding.
generatedNote: The ByteBusters Generative AI Journey is separate from the official coding curriculum. Levels 2–4 were designed by Claude (AI) for review by the ByteBusters team.

weeks.title: From chatbot to agent
weeks.goal: Explain the difference between a chatbot that talks and an agent that takes actions with tools and a plan.
weeks.learn: A chatbot answers questions. An AI agent goes further: it is given a GOAL, TOOLS (like search, a calculator, sending a message), a PLAN of steps, and it repeats 'think, act, check' (green: a loop) until the goal is done. Agents can save time, but because they ACT, mistakes cost more. It's like sending a younger cousin to the market: you give the goal (buy ingredients for jollof), the tools (money, a list, your phone number) and the limits (don't spend above ₦5,000, call me if tomatoes are too costly).

research.q: Ask an adult who sends people on errands (a shop owner, a parent): what instructions do you give so the errand goes well?
research.tip: Write their instructions. They are the same as an agent's goal, tools and limits.

build.task: Fill an Agent Card for a market-errand agent: goal, tools, limits, check-ins.
steps: Read the example Agent Card
Underline the GOAL, circle the TOOLS, box the LIMITS
Write your own Agent Card for a school task (e.g. planning a class party)
Swap with a partner: can they find a missing limit?
build.code:
AGENT CARD
GOAL: Find the best price for ingredients for jollof for 20 people
TOOLS: price search, calculator, shopping list writer
PLAN (repeat until done):
  1. THINK: what do I need next?
  2. ACT: use one tool
  3. CHECK: did it work? If not, try again
LIMITS:
  - Budget: not more than ₦30,000
  - Never pay or send messages without a human's YES
  - Stop and ask if anything is unclear
CHECK-INS: show the plan before starting; show the final list before buying

check.q: What makes an agent different from a chatbot?
opts: It uses tools and takes actions to reach a goal

check.q: 'Think, act, check, repeat' is which logic colour?
Why do agents need LIMITS?
opts: Because they act, and mistakes cost more

weeks.say: A chatbot talks, but an agent acts: it has a goal, tools, a plan and limits, and repeats think-act-check until the job is done.
weeks.safe: An agent must never spend money, send messages or share data without a human saying YES first.

try.ask: Write an agent's instructions: the GOAL, one TOOL and one LIMIT.
try.best: Goal: find the 3 cheapest data plans for our club. Tool: search. Limit: never buy anything, and ask me before you send any message.

trainer.open: Today we meet the next big thing in AI: agents, AIs that DO things, not just talk. You'll learn to be the boss who sends them on errands safely.
plan: Errand game: one kid sends another to 'the market' with only 'buy food'. What goes wrong? Now add goal, tools, limits.
Explain agent = goal + tools + plan loop + limits. Read the Agent Card.
Pairs write an Agent Card for a school task; partners hunt for a missing limit.
lookfor: Names goal, tools and limits correctly
Includes a 'human says YES' limit
Explains the think-act-check loop
fix: Thinks an agent can do anything on its own
Agents only use the tools they're given and only within the limits a human sets.
Writes no money or messaging limits
Ask: what's the worst thing that could happen if it did this without asking you?

weeks.title: Break the goal into steps
weeks.goal: Break a big goal into small, checkable steps that an agent (or a person) can follow one by one.
weeks.learn: Agents work best with small steps. A big goal like 'organise the inter-house sports snack stand' is too vague. Small steps are clear: list snacks, check prices, choose a budget, get approval, buy, set prices, sell. Each step should be checkable: you can tell when it is done. It's like cooking jollof: nobody cooks 'jollof' in one move; you wash rice, blend pepper, fry the stew, add rice, and check it at each stage.

research.q: Ask a cook, tailor or mechanic: what are the steps of one job you do, from start to finish?
research.tip: Count the steps. Experts break big jobs into small steps without thinking about it.

build.task: Build a step tracker that loops through a plan and counts how many steps are done.
steps: Read the 6 steps in the plan list (blue: an array)
Find the loop (green) that puts each step on the screen
Tick steps as done and watch the counter
Change the steps to your own goal
build.code: Goal: Snack stand for inter-house sports

check.q: Which is a good, checkable step?
In the code, what does the for loop do?
opts: Puts each step from the plan on the screen

check.q: Why do agents work better with small steps?
opts: Each step is clear and you can check when it's done

weeks.say: I break a big goal into small steps I can check one by one, so an agent or a person can follow the plan without guessing.
weeks.safe: Put a human approval step before any step that spends money or contacts people.

try.ask: Break this goal into 5 short steps: 'Help our class collect old textbooks for JSS 1 students.'

checks.label: Has an approval or check step

try.best: 1. Ask the principal for permission. 2. Make a poster asking for old textbooks. 3. Collect books at the gate. 4. Sort and check them by subject. 5. Give them to the JSS 1 class teacher.

trainer.open: Big goals scare people, and confuse AI agents. Today you learn the leader's trick: turn any big goal into small, clear steps.
plan: Ask a volunteer to 'cook jollof' in one sentence. Then list the real steps together.
Show what makes a step checkable: you can tell when it's done.
Kids run the tracker, then change the plan to their own goal (6 steps).
Swap phones: can a partner follow your plan? Check questions.
lookfor: Every step starts with a doing word (list, check, buy)
Includes an approval step before spending
Finds the loop in the code
fix: Steps are vague ('prepare well')
Ask: how would I know when 'prepare well' is DONE? Make it something you can see.
Breaks the code by removing quotes or commas in the list
Each step is text in quotes, with a comma between steps.

weeks.title: Human in the loop: you say YES
weeks.goal: Design an agent plan where risky actions wait for a human to approve or stop them.
weeks.learn: Human-in-the-loop means a person must approve important actions before an agent does them. Safe actions (searching, making a list) can run on their own. Risky actions (paying money, sending messages, deleting files, sharing data) must stop and wait for a human YES. A rule decides (red), and a button press is the human's decision (purple). It's like a POS agent who asks you to confirm the amount before pressing 'send', because once money goes, it's hard to bring back.

research.q: Ask a POS agent or bank worker: what do they ALWAYS confirm with the customer before sending money?
research.tip: Write the things they confirm. Your agent needs the same 'confirm before you act' habit.

build.task: Build an approval screen: safe actions run, risky actions wait for Approve or Stop.
steps: Read the 4 actions the agent wants to do
See which are marked risky (red rule)
Press Approve or Stop on each risky one (purple event)
Add one more risky action of your own
build.code: Agent plan: snack stand

check.q: Which action should wait for a human YES?
What does 'human in the loop' mean?
opts: A person approves important actions before the agent does them
A human is stuck inside the computer

check.q: In the code, what decides if an action needs approval?

weeks.say: Safe actions can run on their own, but risky ones like paying or messaging wait for a human to press Approve. I stay in the loop.
weeks.safe: Before you press Approve, read what the agent will do. Approving without reading is the same as no approval.

try.ask: Write a rule for an agent: which actions need a human YES?
try.best: IF the agent wants to pay money, send a message or delete a file THEN it must stop and ask a human to approve first.

trainer.open: Agents are fast, but fast mistakes are still mistakes. Today you design the 'you say YES' button that keeps humans in charge.
plan: POS story: why does the agent confirm the amount before sending?
Sort 8 action cards into SAFE or NEEDS YES as a class.
Kids run the approval screen, then add a new risky action and test it.
Discuss: what if the human just presses Approve without reading? Check questions.
props: 8 action cards (e.g. search, pay, delete, message, list)
lookfor: Sorts money, messages, deleting and sharing as risky
Explains the if (a.risky) rule
Says approval means reading first, not just tapping
fix: Marks everything risky 'to be safe'
Then the human is asked too often and starts tapping YES without reading. Only truly risky actions need a stop.
Thinks approval is the agent's job
The agent can't approve itself. A human must decide.

weeks.title: Check the agent's work
weeks.goal: Verify an agent's report by checking its numbers, sources and actions before you trust it.
weeks.learn: An agent may report 'Done! Total cost ₦14,200', but agents can make mistakes in maths, use old prices, or do extra things nobody asked for. So we verify: redo the important maths, check the sources, and compare what it did with what we asked. It's like counting your change after buying at the market: the seller is usually honest, but you still count before you walk away.

research.q: Ask an adult: have you ever been given the wrong change or a wrong bill? How did you catch it?
research.tip: Write how they caught it. That's a verification habit you can teach an app.

build.task: Build a checker that recalculates the agent's shopping total with a loop.
steps: Read the items list and what the agent claimed (sample prices, not real data)
Find the loop (green) that adds price × quantity
Run it: does the agent's total match?
Change agentSaid to the correct total and run again
build.code: Check the agent's total

check.q: The agent says 'Done!' What should you do?
opts: Check its numbers, sources and actions

check.q: The real total doesn't match what the agent said. Next step?
opts: Don't pay; find and fix the mistake first

check.q: What else should you check besides the maths?
opts: That it didn't do extra things you never asked for

weeks.say: I don't just trust 'Done!' I recheck the maths, check the sources, and make sure the agent did only what I asked.
weeks.safe: Never act on an agent's report (pay, send, publish) until a human has checked it.

try.ask: Write 3 checks you would do before trusting an agent that says it found the cheapest school bus hire.

checks.label: Checks it did only what was asked

try.best: 1. Add up the prices again myself. 2. Call or visit the bus company to confirm the price source. 3. Check it did only what I asked and did not book or pay.

trainer.open: Agents sound very confident, even when they're wrong. Today you become the inspector who counts the change.
plan: Market change role-play: the 'seller' gives wrong change; the class catches it.
List the 3 checks: numbers, sources, actions.
Kids run the checker, find the mismatch, fix agentSaid, and add one new item.
Discuss: what if the agent used last year's prices? Check questions.
lookfor: Recalculates instead of trusting
Finds the ₦1,000 mismatch
Mentions checking sources and extra actions too
fix: Changes the item prices to match the agent
That's hiding the mistake! Fix the report, not the facts.
Thinks checking means asking the agent 'are you sure?'
The agent may just say yes. Check with your own maths and real sources.

weeks.unit: Weeks 5-8 · AI in our school, work and community
weeks.title: Automate a real school task
weeks.goal: Design a safe automation for a real school or community task using WHEN, IF and REPEAT, with a human check.
weeks.learn: An automation is a set of steps that runs by itself when something happens. It has a TRIGGER (purple: WHEN something happens), RULES (red: IF this, THEN that), sometimes a REPEAT (green: every week), and a HUMAN CHECK before anything goes out. Good automations save boring work so people have time for important work. It's like the school bell: nobody has to shout 'break time!'; the bell does it on time every day, but the principal decides the timetable.

research.q: Ask a teacher, club patron or school clerk: what boring task do you repeat every week that a computer could help with?
research.tip: Write the task. A real problem from a real person makes the best automation.

build.task: Write a WHEN-IF-THEN automation plan for a club task; the trainer builds it with a real tool.
steps: Pick a real task from your research
Write the TRIGGER (WHEN), the RULES (IF/THEN) and any REPEAT
Add the HUMAN CHECK before anything is sent
Write what could go wrong and how you'd stop it
Trainer builds it with a school-approved tool and shows the result
build.code:
AUTOMATION PLAN: Weekly ByteBusters reminder
WHEN (trigger): every Monday at 7am  (purple + green repeat)
IF it is a public holiday THEN skip this week  (red)
THEN the AI drafts a short reminder: day, time, what to bring
HUMAN CHECK: the club patron reads and edits it
IF the patron approves THEN send it to the club notice board / parents' group

WHAT COULD GO WRONG?
- Wrong date or time -> the patron checks before sending
- Sends at night -> only send between 7am and 6pm
- Personal data in the message -> never include names or phone numbers

check.q: In an automation, 'every Monday at 7am' is the…
Why add a human check before the reminder is sent?
opts: To slow it down for fun
To catch mistakes before people receive them

check.q: Which task is a good first automation?

weeks.say: My automation runs WHEN something happens, follows IF-THEN rules, and a human checks it before anything is sent.
weeks.safe: Never automate decisions about people (grades, punishments, money) and never automate sending messages without a human check.

try.ask: Write an automation using WHEN, IF and THEN for a school or community task.
try.best: When it is Friday afternoon, the AI drafts a list of next week's club activities. If it is a holiday then skip. The patron must check and approve it before it is posted.

trainer.open: Imagine a helper that never forgets the weekly reminder. Today you design it, and you design the safety checks too.
plan: School bell story: who decides the timetable, and who rings the bell?
Show the plan: label WHEN (purple), IF (red), REPEAT (green), HUMAN CHECK.
Teams write an automation plan for a task from their research, including 'what could go wrong'.
Trainer picks one plan and demos it (e.g. drafting the reminder with AI, then reading it). Check questions.
props: Trainer's phone with an approved tool (e.g. AI chat + a calendar reminder)
lookfor: Plan has a clear trigger and rule
Puts a human check before sending
Names at least one thing that could go wrong
fix: Automates a serious decision about people (punishments, grades)
Decisions about people need human judgement. Automate the boring parts, not the judging.
No plan for what goes wrong
Ask: what if the date is wrong? What if it sends at midnight? Add a rule for it.

weeks.unit: Weeks 5-8 · AI in our school, work and community
weeks.title: AI and jobs in Nigeria
weeks.goal: Interview a local worker to find which parts of their job AI could help with and which parts need a human.
weeks.learn: People worry that AI will take jobs. The truth is more interesting: AI changes TASKS inside jobs. A business-centre typist may type less but design more. A tailor may use AI for pattern ideas but still measures and sews by hand. Some parts need human skills: trust, hands-on work, care and judgement. We find out by asking real workers, not by guessing. It's like when POS machines came: some cashier tasks changed, and new jobs like POS agents appeared.

research.q: Interview one local worker (tailor, mechanic, POS agent, hairdresser, trader, typist): which part of your work is boring or repeated? Which part needs YOU?
research.tip: Write their words. Don't write their name or phone number: just their job and area.

build.task: Fill a Job Task Map from your interview and sort each task.
steps: List 5 tasks the worker does (blue: your data)
Sort each: AI COULD HELP / NEEDS A HUMAN / BOTH
Write one new skill the worker could learn to use AI well
Share with the class; compare different jobs

Each group shares one surprise. Check questions.

weeks.unit: Weeks 5-8 · AI in our school, work and community
weeks.title: Teach the little ones
weeks.goal: Plan and run a 5-minute AI safety lesson for younger pupils, using a simple tap game.
weeks.learn: You learn something best when you teach it. Younger pupils (JSS 1 or primary) are already meeting AI on phones, often with no guide. A peer mentor teaches with simple words, a story and a game, and keeps the rules to 3. Patience matters more than big words. It's like an older sibling teaching a younger one to cross the road: hold hands, look left and right, and practise together.

research.q: Ask a younger child at home (with a parent nearby): have you seen AI on a phone, like Meta AI on WhatsApp? What do you think it is?
research.tip: Write their answer. It shows you where to start your lesson.

build.task: Build a 'Safe or Not?' tap game for younger pupils.
steps: Play the game yourself first
Find the cards list (blue), the score rule (red) and the buttons (purple)
Add one more card that fits our community
Teach it to a younger pupil with your trainer present
build.code: Safe or Not?

check.q: How many rules should a lesson for younger pupils have?
opts: Just a few, like 3, with a game

check.q: A younger pupil gets an answer wrong. What do you do?
opts: Explain kindly with an example and let them try again

check.q: Why does teaching help YOU learn?
opts: You must understand it well enough to explain it simply

weeks.say: I can teach younger pupils 3 AI safety rules with a story and a game, and teaching them makes me understand AI safety better.
weeks.safe: Mentor younger pupils only with your trainer or a teacher present, and never collect their details.

try.ask: Write the 3 AI safety rules you'll teach younger pupils, in very simple words.
try.best: 1. Keep your name, address and phone number secret from AI. 2. Ask a grown-up before you use a new app. 3. AI can be wrong, so check with your teacher.

trainer.open: You've learnt a lot about AI. Now it's your turn to protect younger kids. Today you become a peer mentor.
plan: Older sibling story: how did someone teach you something when you were small?
Agree the 3 rules for little ones: keep secrets secret, check with a grown-up, AI can be wrong.
Kids play the game, add a card, then practise teaching it to a partner who acts as a JSS 1 pupil.
Plan the real mini-lesson with a JSS 1 class (with the trainer). Check questions.
props: Permission arranged with a JSS 1 or primary teacher
lookfor: Uses simple words and a story
Stays patient with wrong answers
Adds a card that is clear and local
fix: Uses big words like 'algorithm' and 'deepfake' with small kids
Ask: would your little cousin understand that word? Say 'a computer that guesses' instead.
Makes the game scary ('AI will steal you')
We want them careful, not afraid. Keep it calm and friendly.

weeks.unit: Weeks 5-8 · AI in our school, work and community
weeks.title: Our club's AI rules
weeks.goal: Write a clear, fair AI-use policy for your ByteBusters club that everyone can follow.
weeks.learn: A policy is a short set of agreed rules. A good AI-use policy says what AI is allowed for, what is NOT allowed, how to credit AI, how to protect privacy, who holds the accounts and keys, and what to do if something goes wrong. Good rules are clear, fair and short enough to remember. Everyone helps write them, so everyone owns them. It's like the rules of a football match: everyone knows them before kick-off, and the referee applies them fairly.

research.q: Ask your school principal, a teacher or a parent: what one rule should every student follow when using AI for schoolwork?
research.tip: Write their rule. Real adults' views make your policy fair to the school, not just to students.

build.task: Write a one-page AI-use policy for your club using the template.
steps: Read the 6 sections of the template
Use your research: what did adults want in the rules?
Write 1-2 IF-THEN rules (red) for each section
Read it aloud: is it clear to a JSS 1 pupil?
Vote to adopt it; the club patron signs
build.code:
BYTEBUSTERS CLUB AI-USE POLICY
1. ALLOWED: We use AI to brainstorm, explain, draft and test.
2. NOT ALLOWED: IF it's an exam or test THEN no AI. No deepfakes of real people.
3. CREDIT: IF AI helped THEN we write what AI did and what we did.
4. PRIVACY: We never type names, numbers, addresses or photos of people into AI.
5. ACCOUNTS & KEYS: Only the trainer holds AI accounts and API keys.
6. IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG: IF AI shows something harmful or upsetting THEN stop and tell the trainer at once.

Agreed by the club on ___   Patron: ___

check.q: What makes a good policy?
opts: Long and full of hard words
Clear, fair and short enough to remember

check.q: Who should hold AI accounts and API keys in the club?
AI shows something upsetting. Our policy says…
opts: Stop and tell the trainer at once

weeks.say: Our club's AI policy is short, clear and fair: what's allowed, what's not, how to credit, how to protect privacy, who holds keys, and what to do if something goes wrong.
weeks.safe: Our policy protects people first: privacy, honesty, and telling an adult when something is wrong.

try.ask: Write 2 rules for your club's AI-use policy using IF ... THEN.
try.best: IF AI helped with our project THEN we write what AI did and what we did. IF a prompt needs a name or phone number THEN we leave it out to protect privacy.

trainer.open: Today you're the lawmakers! You'll write the AI rules for our own club, and because you write them, you'll keep them.
plan: Football rules chat: what happens in a match with no agreed rules?
Show the 6 sections. Share research: what rules did adults suggest?
Groups each write one section; combine them into one policy on the board.
Read it aloud, vote, and the patron signs. Check questions.
props: A marker for the patron to sign
lookfor: Rules are specific and testable
Includes privacy and keys
Listens to others' suggestions and votes fairly
fix: Rules are too strict to follow ('never touch AI')
Rules people can't keep get ignored. Make them fair and realistic.
Rules are vague ('use AI well')
Ask: how would the referee know if someone broke this rule? Make it clear.

weeks.title: Capstone: AI for a real local need
weeks.goal: Plan a capstone AI project for a real need in your community, with users, steps, safety rules and a test plan.
weeks.learn: Your capstone brings everything together: a REAL problem from real people, a small AI tool or agent plan that helps, safety rules, human checks, and a test plan. Keep it small and doable: one problem, one group of users, one clear result. Use the trainer's AI account for building (e.g. honest vibe-coding with Claude). It's like a final-year project at a polytechnic: not the biggest idea, but the one you can build, test and defend well.

research.q: Ask 5 people in one group (traders, farmers, parents, teachers): what problem takes your time every week that information could help with?
research.tip: Pick the problem that 3 or more people mention. That's your evidence that the need is real.

build.task: Fill the Capstone Plan and write the planning prompt the trainer will use with the AI.
steps: Choose the problem from your research (the need)
Fill the plan: users, what the tool does, data, rules, human check, test
Write the planning prompt (bottom) and ask your trainer to run it with Claude
Choose the smallest version you can build in 2 weeks
build.code:
CAPSTONE PLAN
NEED (from research): Farmers in our area guess when to spray, then rain washes it off
USERS: small farmers near Ilaro
TOOL: shows tomorrow's rain chance (free Open-Meteo API) + an AI tip in Yoruba or English
DATA: area name only (no names, no numbers)
RULES: IF rain chance is high THEN advise waiting. IF unsure THEN say 'ask an extension worker'
HUMAN CHECK: a farmer and the trainer check AI tips before launch
TEST: 10 inputs (Level 3 test set) + 5 real farmers

PLANNING PROMPT (trainer runs it):
I want to build a small, safe tool that helps {users} with {need}.
Before any code, ask me 5 questions. Then give a simple plan: inputs (variables),
rules (if-then), repeats (loops) and buttons (events). Use simple words. I am 15
and I must explain every part to judges.

check.q: Where should your capstone problem come from?
opts: Real people who face the problem every week

check.q: Your idea is very big. What should you do?
opts: Build the smallest version that still helps

check.q: Why ask the AI to ask YOU 5 questions first?
opts: So the plan fits the real need and you understand it

weeks.say: My capstone solves a real local need. I planned the users, data, rules, human checks and tests, and I chose a small version I can build and explain.
weeks.safe: Your capstone must collect the least data possible, keep keys with the trainer, and be checked by real users before launch.

try.best: I want to build a small, safe tool that helps {users} with {need}. Before any code, ask me 5 questions. Then give me a simple plan with inputs, rules, loops and buttons, in simple words.

trainer.open: This is the big one: your capstone. Today you plan an AI project for a real need, small enough to build and strong enough to defend.

Walk through the farmer example plan. Point out the 4 colours in it.
Teams fill their Capstone Plan and the planning prompt. Trainer runs one prompt with Claude live.
Each team says its need and smallest version in one sentence. Check questions.

Plan includes rules, a human check and a test
Picks a small, buildable version
fix: 'Our app will end poverty in Nigeria'
Great dream! Now shrink it: which ONE group, ONE problem, ONE result can you show in 2 weeks?
Plan collects personal data 'to make it better'

weeks.title: Defend it: the 5 signs
weeks.goal: Defend your capstone to judges with the 5 signs of understanding, real-user evidence and your safety choices.
weeks.learn: Judges don't just want to see that your project works; they want proof that YOU understand it. The 5 signs are: PURPOSE (the problem and who it helps), HOW IT WORKS (button, prompt, API or agent steps, answer), LOGIC (a variable, a rule, a loop, an event), MY DECISIONS (what you chose and why, including AI you directed), and CHANGE IT (what you'd improve and how). Add your safety and leadership story: approvals, privacy, policy, mentoring. It's like a lawyer in court: facts, evidence and calm answers.

research.q: Do a practice defence for 2 adults (a parent, a teacher). Ask them to ask you the hardest question they can think of.
research.tip: Write their question and your best answer. Judges often ask the same kind.

build.task: Prepare and practise your 90-second capstone defence with the 5 signs.
steps: Fill each of the 5 signs in 1-2 sentences
Add one piece of real-user evidence and one safety choice
Practise 3 times; a partner ticks each sign they hear
Answer 2 tough judge questions from your partner
Final: defend to the class or the visiting judges
build.code:
MY 90-SECOND DEFENCE
1. PURPOSE: The problem is ___ and it helps ___
2. HOW IT WORKS: When the user ___, the app/agent ___, then ___
3. LOGIC: variable ___ | rule (IF) ___ | loop ___ | event ___
4. MY DECISIONS: I chose ___ because ___. I directed the AI to ___ and checked ___

EVIDENCE: A real user said: '___'
SAFETY & LEADERSHIP: human approval for ___; privacy: ___; our club policy: ___
